title: Snapped Cable or Broken Spring? How to Tell Which One You Have
description: A loud bang, a door that won't budge, or a door hanging crooked — here's how to tell a broken garage door cable from a broken spring, and what to do (and not do) next.
imageAlt: Brown raised-panel double garage door on a brick home
keywords: broken garage door cable vs spring, garage door won't open bang, garage door cable snapped, garage door spring broken, garage door hanging crooked
h1: Snapped Cable or Broken Spring? How to Tell Which One You Have
intro: You heard a bang, or you just noticed the door won't move right, and now you're standing in the garage trying to figure out what actually broke. Cables and springs fail in different ways, and telling them apart matters — not because the fix is wildly different for you (either way, hands off), but because knowing what you're dealing with tells you how urgent it is and what to expect when a technician shows up. Here's how to read the signs.

sections.heading: The quickest tell: where the broken part is
sections.body:
Start by looking at the two obvious locations. The spring (or springs) is the tightly wound coil mounted on a shaft above the closed door, running horizontally across the top of the opening — or, on older doors, a pair of long thinner coils stretched along the upper tracks on each side. The cables are the braided steel lines running down the sides of the door, from the drums near the spring assembly down to the bottom corner brackets.

If you can see a clean gap in that horizontal coil above the door, or one half of it has visibly sprung away from the other, that's a broken spring. If the coil above the door looks intact but you see a loose, frayed, or detached steel line running down one side of the door — or the cable has come off its drum entirely — that's a cable failure. Don't touch either one to get a closer look; looking is fine, reaching in is not.

sections.heading: What a broken spring looks and sounds like
sections.body:
A spring failure is usually loud and sudden — many homeowners describe it as a gunshot or a car backfiring inside the garage, sometimes with the house shaking slightly. After that, the door becomes dramatically heavy. If the opener was mid-cycle, it may strain, stall, or reverse. If the door was already down, it may look completely normal from the outside — the tell is that it won't lift, or the opener strains hard and only gets it a few inches before giving up.

A door with a broken spring sitting closed can look deceptively fine. The problem shows up the moment anyone tries to operate it, because the opener was never designed to lift the door's full weight on its own — it only ever had to overcome the small amount of force the spring didn't already counterbalance. Take away the spring and the opener is trying to lift what is often 150 pounds or more of steel.

sections.heading: What a snapped or failing cable looks and sounds like
sections.body:
Cable failure tends to be less dramatic and more lopsided. Instead of one loud bang, you're more likely to notice the door hanging crooked — one bottom corner lower than the other, or a visible gap under one side when it's supposed to be sealed. A cable that's failing but hasn't fully snapped yet often shows fraying (loose steel strands sticking out near the bottom bracket) or looks slack and floppy compared to its twin on the other side.

If a cable fully lets go while the door is moving, you may hear a sharper snap or clatter rather than a boom, and the door can drop unevenly or jam diagonally in the tracks mid-cycle. That uneven drop is actually the more damage-prone failure mode of the two — a door that jams crooked in its tracks can bend panels and rollers in the process, which a clean spring failure usually doesn't do by itself.

sections.heading: Why the two often show up together
sections.body: Cables and springs aren't independent parts — they work the same system and tend to age on the same clock. The cables carry the spring's lifting force to the door, so a spring nearing the end of its rated cycle life puts uneven, jerkier load on the cables with every operation, which accelerates cable wear. That's exactly why a technician diagnosing a snapped cable will also check spring condition, and why a spring replacement call is a good moment to have cables inspected even if they haven't failed yet. If you're seeing signs of one, don't assume the other is fine just because it hasn't failed — ask to have both checked in the same visit.

sections.heading: What to do right now, regardless of which one it is
sections.body:
The immediate steps are the same either way:

1. **Stop operating the door.** Don't press the opener button repeatedly to "see if it'll go" — on a cable failure this is how a crooked door becomes a bent-panel, bent-track repair. On a spring failure, it's how an opener motor or drive gear gets damaged trying to lift weight it wasn't built for.
2. **Don't disconnect the opener and try to lift it manually** unless you already know the spring is intact — a door with a failed spring can be far heavier than it looks, and if you're not sure which part failed, treat it as if the spring did.
3. **Keep the area clear.** Both parts are under significant tension even when they're not actively failing. A broken spring half or a loose cable end can move unpredictably.
4. **Call for service** and describe what you saw and heard — a loud bang versus a crooked door versus a cable you can see fraying all point a technician toward a faster, more accurate diagnosis before they even arrive.

sections.heading: What repair looks like for each
sections.body:
Spring replacement generally runs **$175 to $350** in our service area, depending on whether it's a torsion or extension system and whether it's a single- or double-spring door. Cable and roller work falls in the standard repair range, **$150 to $300**. Both are typically same-visit repairs — technicians carry the common sizes on the truck — and both come with our 1-year parts & labor warranty.

One rule applies to both parts: replace in pairs. If one spring or one cable failed, its twin has the same age and wear history and is usually not far behind. Replacing only the failed half is a common way to end up paying for a second service call within months. A balance test at the end of the job — the door stays put at about half-height without drifting — is the real proof the repair was done correctly, whichever part was replaced.

faq.question: How do I know if it's my garage door spring or cable that broke?
faq.answer: Look at the horizontal coil above the closed door — a visible gap or separated coil means a broken spring, often with a loud bang at the moment of failure. If that coil looks intact but you see a loose, frayed, or detached steel line down one side of the door, or the door is hanging crooked, that points to a cable problem instead.

faq.question: Why did my garage door make a loud bang and then not open?
faq.answer: A loud bang followed by a door that won't lift, or an opener that strains and stalls, is the classic sign of a broken spring. The spring normally carries almost all of the door's weight; without it, the opener is trying to lift hundreds of pounds on its own and can't.

faq.question: Can I open my garage door manually if the spring or cable is broken?
faq.answer: We don't recommend it. If the spring failed, the door can be far heavier than it looks and difficult or dangerous to lift by hand. If a cable failed, pulling on the door can cause it to drop unevenly or jam diagonally in the tracks, which risks bending panels. Leave the door as it is and call for service.

faq.question: Is a broken cable or a broken spring more urgent?
faq.answer: Both deserve prompt attention, but a cable failure can cause additional damage faster — a door that jams crooked in the tracks while someone keeps trying to operate it can bend panels and rollers. Either way, stop using the door and call rather than testing it repeatedly.
